extracted.intended_audience: readers of Darwin's correspondence; historians of science; evolutionary biologists and naturalists interested in 19th-century scientific method and practice
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting evaluative rules, methodological advice, and disciplinary judgments embedded in Charles Darwin's letters about natural history, variation, distribution, and scientific practice. The page is primary-source correspondence illustrating criteria Darwin used to judge evidence, publication strategy, collecting priorities, and awards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base theorizing on long-continued study and practical acquaintance
rubrics_metrics.description: All my notions about HOW species change are derived from long continued study of the works of (and converse with) agriculturists and horticulturists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give weight to prolonged empirical study and sustained practical experience (e.g., agricultural and horticultural observations) when forming hypotheses about species change; practical/domestic knowledge can be essential evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim to uncover 'laws of change' to make Natural History a science
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever it is proved that all species are produced by generation, by laws of change, what good evidence we shall have of the gaps in formations. And what a science Natural History will be, when ... all the laws of change are thought one of the most important parts of Natural History.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize identifying general laws governing variation and change; work that elucidates such laws is what will transform natural history into a mature science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species-naming criterion: amount of difference and permanence
rubrics_metrics.description: I should only have thought whether the amount of difference and permanence was sufficient to justify a name... I differ from him greatly in thinking that those who believe that species are NOT fixed will multiply specific names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not multiply species names lightly; base taxonomic naming on demonstrable degree of difference and stability (permanence) rather than on a priori assumptions about creation or fixity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer hypotheses consistent with broad distributional facts (skepticism of continental extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: I cannot get over the fact that not a fragment of secondary or palaeozoic rock has been found on any island above 500 or 600 miles from a mainland... the generality of the facts of all islands (except one or two) having a considerable part of their productions in common with one or more mainlands utterly staggers me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate geological or biogeographical hypotheses against wide-ranging distributional evidence; reject (or remain skeptical of) hypotheses—e.g., large-scale continental extension—if they conflict with consistent empirical distribution patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use domesticated varieties and old literature as key evidence for variation
rubrics_metrics.description: I have found my careful work at pigeons really invaluable, as enlightening me on many points on variation under domestication. The copious old literature, by which I can trace the gradual changes in the breeds of pigeons has been extraordinarily useful to me.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage documented cases of domestication and historical literature to trace gradual changes and infer principles of variation; domestic breeds can be model systems for understanding variability and selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication strategy: prefer a full, material-backed work over premature sketches
rubrics_metrics.description: When I began I found it such unsatisfactory work that I have desisted, and am now drawing up my work as perfect as my materials of nineteen years' collecting suffice... I have found it quite impossible to publish any preliminary essay or sketch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid publishing premature sketches; prepare comprehensive works grounded in available materials rather than fragmentary outlines—unless compelled otherwise by special circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirically test mechanisms of dispersal rather than rely on mere possibility
rubrics_metrics.description: No subject gives me so much trouble and doubt and difficulty as the means of dispersal... I cannot anyhow get their eggs to experimentise their power of floating and resistance to the injurious action of salt water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and carry out experiments (e.g., egg-floating, salt-water resistance) to test proposed dispersal mechanisms; do not rest content with listing merely possible means of distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'specific centre' may be small and human-influenced locales
rubrics_metrics.description: I should call the kitchen garden in which the red cabbage was produced, or the farm in which Bakewell made the Shorthorn cattle, the specific centre of these SPECIES! And surely this is centralisation enough!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying centers of origin or specific centres, accept small, anthropogenic or domestication-associated localities (gardens, farms) as legitimate centres for the origin of varieties or breeds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causal inference in variation: external conditions vs selection/time
rubrics_metrics.description: My conclusion... is that external conditions (to which naturalists so often appeal) do by themselves VERY LITTLE. ... The formation of a strong variety or species I look as almost wholly due to the selection of what may be incorrectly called CHANCE variations or variability. This power of selection stands in the most direct relation to time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining formation of varieties/species, emphasize selection acting on variation over long timescales and the role of biotic associates; treat direct climatic or external conditions as generally minor causes except where proven otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate observations by observer quality and be wary of bad observers
rubrics_metrics.description: I have sometimes thought that (quite independently of the present case), you are a little too hard on bad observers; that a remark made by a bad observer CANNOT be right... I feel entire deference to any remark you make out of your own head; but when in opposition to some poor devil, I somehow involuntarily feel not quite so much.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the credibility of empirical claims by considering the observer's reliability and competence; treat reports from poorly trained or unreliable observers with caution, while still weighing all evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of compilation as serious scientific work
rubrics_metrics.description: Depend on it, my saying is a true one, viz., that a compiler is a GREAT man, and an original man a commonplace man. Any fool can generalise and speculate; but, oh, my heavens! To get up AT SECOND HAND a New Zealand Flora, that is work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize comprehensive compilation and careful synthesis of existing data (e.g., floras, faunas) as valuable and demanding scientific labor—not merely derivative or second-rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize careful collecting on isolated/poorly-known islands
rubrics_metrics.description: It is my most deliberate conviction that nothing would aid more, Natural History, than careful collecting and investigating ALL THE PRODUCTIONS of the most isolated islands, especially of the southern hemisphere... What grand work to explore Rodriguez, with its fossil birds, and little known productions of every kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate expeditionary resources to thorough sampling of isolated, understudied islands (flora, fauna, geology); include dredging and search for fossils—these localities can yield disproportionately important data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awarding medals and honors: favor young workers and guard against lax criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an old notion of mine that more good is done by giving medals to younger men in the early part of their career, than as a mere reward to men whose scientific career is nearly finished... if general claims are once admitted, it opens the door to great laxity in giving them... Think of the case of a very rich man, who aided SOLELY with his money... Would you give such men medals?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When setting award criteria, consider prioritizing recognition for promising early-career investigators; keep the basis for awards specific to prevent laxity, and debate whether financial benefactors or purely honorary claims should receive scientific medals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predict variability: highly developed or unusual organs tend to be more variable
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposition that any part or organ developed normally (i.e., not a monstrosity) in a species in any HIGH or UNUSUAL degree, compared with the same part or organ in allied species, tends to be HIGHLY VARIABLE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence of unusually developed structures (relative to close allies) as a predictor of high variability; test this hypothesis across taxa and use it to guide searches for variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for precise measurement and quantitative data in botanical variation
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of botanical facts may in part be accounted for by the difficulty of measuring slight variations... How different, for instance, from the beak of a bird! ... I never dreamed that you had kept the subject at all before your mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize methodological limits in detecting slight plant variation; employ precise, quantitative measurement methods to assess variability in botanical characters, since casual notes may miss subtle but important variation.
